questions.stem: Which of the following best defines business ethics?
options: The moral principles that guide how a business behaves, beyond what the law requires
The laws a business must obey in each country where it operates
The accounting standards used to prepare accounts
The rules set by the WTO for international trade
questions.why: Ethics lives in the gap between what is legal and what is right, which is where this whole topic sits.
whyNot: Law is the minimum, not the standard.
Those govern reporting.
Those govern trade between governments.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines sustainability?
options: Meeting present needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs
Maintaining a business's profit at a constant level
Using only locally sourced materials
Recycling all packaging waste
questions.why: The commercial case is often strong, because depleting the resource destroys the business.
whyNot: That is profit stability.
That is local sourcing.
Recycling is one action within sustainability.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines child labour?
options: The employment of children in work that deprives them of schooling or harms their development
Any employment of a person under 18
Employment of children in family businesses only
The employment of children at below the minimum wage
questions.why: Some standards, such as safety and the prohibition of child labour, are not matters of local preference.
whyNot: Some supervised work above a minimum age is lawful and not harmful.
It is not limited to family businesses.
The pay level is not the defining feature.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a race to the bottom?
options: Competition between countries to attract investment by lowering labour, tax or environmental standards
Competition between businesses to offer the lowest prices
The fall in a currency's value against others
A decline in a country's GDP per capita
questions.why: Each government's action is individually rational and all end up worse off.
whyNot: That is price competition.
That is depreciation.
That is falling income per head.

questions.stem: Which conflict defines international business ethics?
options: Customers wanting low prices against workers in the supply chain wanting decent pay
Shareholders wanting dividends against managers wanting bonuses
Governments wanting tax against consumers wanting choice
Suppliers wanting prompt payment against lenders wanting interest
questions.why: It cannot be resolved by good intentions, because the low price depends on the low wage.
whyNot: That is a domestic governance conflict.
That is a policy tension, not the defining ethical conflict.
Both are financial claims rather than the central conflict.

questions.stem: Why can a business not disclaim responsibility for its suppliers' conduct?
options: Customers hold the brand responsible, and the business benefits from the low cost
Contracts with suppliers are legally unenforceable
Suppliers are legally part of the business
Suppliers cannot be audited
questions.why: The business has the commercial power in the relationship, so it has the practical ability to set conditions.
whyNot: Supplier contracts are enforceable.
They are separate legal entities.
Audits are possible, though they can be evaded.

questions.stem: Why is withdrawing from a supplier often not the ethical response?
options: Cancelling the order removes the workers' income and does nothing about the conditions
Withdrawal is prohibited by supply contracts
Withdrawal always costs more than compliance
Withdrawal transfers legal liability to the business
questions.why: Requiring improvement and verifying it usually does more good than leaving, which is a genuinely sophisticated point.
whyNot: Contracts can normally be ended on notice.
Cost varies; the objection is about the workers.
Liability is not created by withdrawal.

questions.stem: Why does auditing tier one of a supply chain not reveal what happens at tier three?
options: A first-tier supplier subcontracts, and the subcontractor subcontracts again
Tier three suppliers are always in a different country
Audits are prohibited beyond the first tier
Tier three suppliers do not employ any workers
questions.why: Long and opaque supply chains are the main practical difficulty in supply chain ethics.
whyNot: They may be in the same country.
Mapping beyond tier one is possible, just difficult.
They employ workers, which is the concern.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a marketing ethics issue named in the specification?
options: Misleading product labelling
Selling at a premium price
Advertising in more than one language
Sponsoring a sports team
questions.why: Inappropriate marketing activities is the other named marketing consideration.
whyNot: Premium pricing is not in itself unethical.
Multilingual advertising is ordinary practice.
Sponsorship is a legitimate promotional activity.

questions.stem: What is the double standard that defines international business ethics?
options: Doing abroad what would not be permitted at home, justified because local law allows it
Charging different prices in different countries
Applying different accounting standards in different subsidiaries
Paying managers more than production workers
questions.why: It is the single most useful framing for an essay on international business ethics.
whyNot: Price discrimination is a commercial practice.
Reporting standards vary legitimately by jurisdiction.
Pay differentials are normal, though their scale raises separate questions.

questions.stem: Why is greenwashing worse than making no environmental claim?
options: The gap between the claim and the behaviour becomes the story
Environmental claims are unlawful in most countries
Greenwashing costs more than genuine action
It prevents a business from advertising at all
questions.why: A business judged on its behaviour is in a better position than one caught claiming more than it delivers.
whyNot: Claims are lawful provided they are not misleading.
It is usually cheaper, which is why it happens.
It does not remove the ability to advertise.

questions.stem: When does the conflict between ethics and profit largely disappear?
options: Where the resource being protected is itself the business, such as a reef or a fishery
Where the business is very large
Where the business has a strong brand
Where regulation in the host country is weak
questions.why: Damaging the asset destroys the business, so an environmental standard becomes a commercial policy.
whyNot: Size does not resolve the conflict.
A strong brand raises the reputational stake but does not remove the trade-off.
Weak regulation widens the gap rather than closing it.

questions.stem: What does responsible supply chain practice look like?
options: A published code, mapping beyond tier one, unannounced audits and remediation rather than termination
A published code with an annual self-assessment
Switching to the lowest-price supplier each year
Relying on the supplier's own assurances
questions.why: Long-term relationships and paying enough to make compliance possible are also part of it.
whyNot: Self-assessment with no verification is a public relations document.
Lowest-price switching removes any leverage to improve conditions.
Assurances without verification are not practice.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an honest argument against applying home standards worldwide?
options: It costs more, and competitors who do not do it have lower costs
Home standards are always inappropriate abroad
Local workers prefer poor conditions
Ethical standards reduce product quality
questions.why: Acknowledging the genuine difficulties makes the answer stronger, not weaker.
whyNot: Some standards, such as safety, are not local preferences.
That is not a credible claim.
Higher standards generally improve quality.

questions.stem: Why is the stated willingness of customers to pay more for ethical products a weak foundation?
options: Stated willingness consistently exceeds actual purchasing behaviour
Customers are unaware that ethical issues exist
Ethical products cannot be priced higher
Willingness to pay cannot be measured
questions.why: The gap between what customers say and do undermines the commercial case for ethical premiums.
whyNot: Awareness is generally high.
They can be, but the volume may not follow.
It is measured routinely, which is how the gap is known.

questions.stem: In a remote island resort, which labour issue raises the ethical questions?
options: Rest days, accommodation quality, family contact and pay relative to guest rates
The legality of employing foreign nationals
Whether guests tip staff directly
The currency in which staff are paid
questions.why: The short-run cost is real and the long-run return comes through retention, which matters where a specialist cannot be replaced mid-season.
whyNot: That is an immigration compliance matter.
Tipping arrangements are a minor operational detail.
Payment currency is an administrative matter.

questions.stem: What is the honest overall conclusion on international business ethics?
options: In the short run ethics costs money; over a long enough horizon reputation and retention usually outweigh it
Ethical behaviour always increases profit immediately
Ethical behaviour always reduces profit permanently
Ethics and profit are entirely unrelated
questions.why: Short run against long run is the distinction that organises the whole judgement.
whyNot: The short-run cost is real and should be acknowledged.
Over time, reputation, retention and avoided scandal usually pay.
They are closely connected, which is why the topic is examinable.
